name: Shock: Types, Stages and Tissue Effects

reference.source: Robbins Basic Pathology 9th Edition (topic map; text rewritten, no verbatim copy)
clinicalPearls: Shock is hypoperfusion, not just low blood pressure
Warm shock suggests distributive sepsis; cold shock suggests low volume or pump failure
Lactate tracks anaerobic metabolism and severity
Acute tubular necrosis is the classic renal lesion of prolonged shock
reference.pathophysiology: Falling oxygen delivery forces anaerobic glycolysis, lactate accumulation and acidosis. Compensatory vasoconstriction protects heart and brain at the cost of gut, kidney and skin. Sustained hypoxia damages endothelium, activates coagulation and inflammation, and progresses to irreversible membrane failure.
additionalDifferentials: Early warm septic shock versus cold shock
additionalInvestigations: Serial lactate and blood gas measurement
Urine output and mentation as perfusion markers
Echocardiography and ultrasound to classify mechanism
